_doc: Hand-curated organizations (Michiko, 2026-11-01). Each org's members, roles and citations are set here and win over the automatic org finder. 'drop' lists automatic labels whose members are replaced by these curated lists. Curated orgs are always shown, even with zero or one member.

orgs.name: Vigilant Committee to suppress crime (1822)
orgs.note: An anti-crime, law-and-order committee formed in 1822, with Richard Allen as chairman and Russell Parrott as secretary (Poulson's, March 2, 1822). A different body from the later vigilance committees that aided fugitives. Members as listed in Julie Winch's reference entries. The Philadelphia Inquirer (Mar. 6, 1822) reported it as a committee of vigilance, thirty in number, appointed at a numerous meeting at Bethel Church to co-operate with the Mayor and police (Newspapers.com clipping). Clipping: clippings/PI_1822-03-06_p2_committee-of-vigilance.jpg Newspapers.com article, The Philadelphia Inquirer, Bethel Church: https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-philadelphia-inquirer-bethel-church/209537487/

orgs.name: Committee of Vigilance to support the Rights of All (1829)
orgs.note: Appointed at a meeting chaired by Benjamin Paschal Jr. to support Samuel Cornish's newspaper The Rights of All (Rights of All, Oct. 9, 1829). Members as listed in Julie Winch's reference entries.

orgs.name: Vigilant Committee of Philadelphia (1837)
orgs.note: Founded in 1837 to aid people escaping slavery. Winch's sources call it both the Vigilance Committee and the Vigilance Association: James McCrummell president (later Robert Purvis), James Needham treasurer, Jacob White secretary, with a standing committee. Active into the 1840s. Members as listed in Julie Winch's reference entries. Dr. James J. G. Bias is linked from Winch notes that are filed under Eliza A. Bias but describe him (cupper, later dentist, 2 Acorn Alley). The Pennsylvania Freeman (June 20, 1839) printed the officers elected May 31, 1839: Robert Purvis president, Edwin H. Coats vice president, James Needham treasurer, Robert B. Ayres secretary, Jacob C. White agent, with a standing committee of twelve, and the financial committee chosen June 10 (Purvis, Edward Needles, Joseph Healy, Samuel Levick). The committee's minute book names the standing committee: James Gibbons, George W. Steward, James J. G. Bias, Joseph Healy, Walter Proctor, Shephard Shay, Stephen H. Gloucester, Westward F. Keeling, Ralph Smith, Samuel Hastings, Daniel Colly and Samuel Levick; its roll later replaces Proctor with Rowland Johnson and Keeling with Edward Needles (Vigilant Committee of Philadelphia Records (Am .3375), Leon Gardiner Collection, Historical Society of Pennsylvania). Clipping: clippings/PF_1839-06-20_p2_vigilant-association-officers.jpg Minute book, p. 27: manuscripts/VCP_1839/HSP_LGC_VCP_minutes_p27.jpg Minute book, p. 25: manuscripts/VCP_1839/HSP_LGC_VCP_minutes_p25.jpg Digitized minute book (1838 Black Metropolis): https://online.flippingbook.com/view/485219936/26-27/

orgs.name: Female Vigilant Committee
orgs.note: The Female Vigilant Association of Philadelphia, founded 1838: Elizabeth White president, Sarah McCrummell treasurer, Ruth Harding secretary (Pennsylvania Freeman, July 5, 1838). It raised money and aid alongside the men's Vigilant Committee but was its own organization. Charles W. Gardner addressed it in 1840. Its constitution says its funds were to carry out the objects of the Vigilant Association of Philadelphia, and its own Vigilant Committee of Fifteen was to act in concert with the Philadelphia Vigilant Committee (Pennsylvania Freeman, July 5, 1838). Its Christmas fair opened Monday, Dec. 24, 1838 in the School Room on Locust Street above 8th, opposite the Musical Fund Hall, to gather funds for the poor and distressed (Pennsylvania Freeman, Dec. 20, 1838, p. 3). orgs.name: Special Vigilance Committee (1851)
orgs.note: Formed in late 1851, after the Christiana resistance, to aid fugitives (Frederick Douglass' Paper, Nov. 13, 1851; Voice of the Fugitive, Jan. 15 and Feb. 12, 1852). Members as listed in Julie Winch's reference entries. Its report on the Christiana cases, signed by Nath'l W. Depee, Secretary, Feb. 10, 1852, and printed in Frederick Douglass' Paper, March 4, 1852 (p. 1, col. 3), shows it hiring legal counsel for the Christiana defendants, supporting the 25 prisoners through four months in jail, aiding their families, sending Geo. Williams and Jacob Moore and their families to Canada, and boarding the witnesses during the trials. It raised $689.41 from Philadelphia churches (Bethel gave $73.50) and beneficial societies, and from donors as far as San Francisco. Courtesy New York Heritage Digital Collections, St. John Fisher University. orgs.name: Vigilance Committee of 1852 (William Still)
orgs.note: The committee William Still worked through after 1852, as remembered by William Carl Bolivar (Pencil Pusher Points, Philadelphia Tribune, Aug. 23, 1913): John P. Burr, Rev. Jeremiah Asher, N. Depee, William Still, I. C. Wear, Jacob C. White and Charles Wise.

orgs.name: Frank Johnson Guards
orgs.note: A Black militia company in Philadelphia. In 1859 it assembled and marched armed through the city. Amos Webber described the march in his diary, and the Daily Ledger objected that only white men could legally keep military companies; The Baltimore Sun's Philadelphia correspondent reported the parade of Aug. 16, 1859 under Capt. Henry Cropper, 'from Liberia': the company's second parade but the first with arms, in dark blue uniform with white pants, belts and cartridge boxes, with martial music. 'There is a law of the State confining military organizations to white men, and therefore the parade yesterday creates considerable remark' (Baltimore Sun, Aug. 18, 1859, p. 4; Newspapers.com clipping). Source: 1838 Black Metropolis blog post on Samuel Williams, https://www.1838blackmetropolis.com/post/williams Clipping: clippings/BS_1859-08-18_p4_frank-johnson-guards.jpg

orgs.name: Williams Assembly (1865)
orgs.note: Founded in 1865 by Samuel Williams specifically for protection. Its constitution speaks of 'protection' rather than the 'mutual relief' of ordinary beneficial societies; members were barred from gambling, profanity and public drunkenness, and it had a Marshall and bought badges, at a time when no Black man could join the Philadelphia police (until William Dicks in 1884). Source: 1838 Black Metropolis blog post on Samuel Williams, https://www.1838blackmetropolis.com/post/williams

orgs.name: Agricultural and Mechanics Association of Pennsylvania and New Jersey
orgs.note: A Black-led stock association founded in Philadelphia on May 1, 1839, with $10 shares. Its constitution allowed the treasurer to put share money toward buying land, stock, materials and fixtures, and toward agents and teachers. Jacob C. White Sr. kept its stock book and accounts and served as treasurer. Many of its subscribers were also active in the Vigilant Committee and the Female Vigilant Committee. Source: constitution and stock book, Leon Gardiner Collection, Historical Society of Pennsylvania; 1838 Black Metropolis blog, https://www.1838blackmetropolis.com/site/post/finding-black-led-creation-and-use-of-economic-instruments-to-support-freedom-seekers-in-1840/

orgs.name: Committee of Vigilance against kidnapping (1827)
orgs.note: Appointed at Bethel Church in February 1827, after Richard Allen read the congregation Mayor Joseph Watson's notice about Philadelphia children kidnapped and sold into slavery in the South: 'a committee of vigilance consisting of twenty persons of colour... to aid in the detection of those offenders, and to give all and every necessary information to the civil authorities of this city.' A public meeting at Bethel on Monday, Feb. 5, 1827 took up the abductions. Its twenty members are not named in the report. The Philadelphia Inquirer (Feb. 3 and 5, 1827) announced the meeting, and the United States Gazette (Feb. 23, 1827, p. 4) reported the committee (Newspapers.com clippings). Clipping: clippings/USG_1827-02-23_p4_committee-of-vigilance.jpg Clipping: clippings/PI_1827-02-03_p2_kidnapping-meeting.jpg Clipping: clippings/PI_1827-02-05_p3_kidnapping-meeting.jpg Connected to the Protecting Society of the City and County of Philadelphia: we cannot be absolutely sure, but we think the two are connected. The Protecting Society appears to have developed out of the need shown at the February 1827 meeting at Bethel and by this committee; its notices appear in Freedom's Journal from April 1828 (dated Philadelphia, April 24, 1828). The two are kept as separate entries (Michiko Quinones, 2026-11-03).

orgs.name: Protecting Society of the City and County of Philadelphia
orgs.note: The Protecting Society of the City and County of Philadelphia for the preventing of Kidnapping and Man-stealing, auxiliary to the Abolition Society, formed in 1827. Its notices appear in Freedom's Journal from April 1828 (dated Philadelphia, April 24, 1828), signed by John Allen, Secretary, Richard Allen's son. Connected to the Committee of Vigilance against kidnapping (1827): we cannot be absolutely sure, but we think the two are connected. The Protecting Society appears to have developed out of the need shown at the February 1827 meeting at Bethel on the kidnappings and by the committee of vigilance appointed there. The two are kept as separate entries (Michiko Quinones, 2026-11-03). Notice: Freedom's Journal, May 16, 1828, p. 7. Clipping: clippings/FJ_1828-05-16_p7_protecting-society-notice.jpg

orgs.name: African Insurance Company
orgs.note: A Black-owned insurance company with its office at No. 159 Lombard Street, capital of 5,000 dollars in 50-dollar shares. In 1811 its president was Joseph Randolph, its treasurer Cyrus Porter and its secretary William Coleman, and the directory notes that 'The members of this company are all coloured persons' (The Philadelphia Directory for 1811, p. 416). Treasurer Cyrus Porter, a stablekeeper, lived at 159 Lombard, the company's office. Julie Winch's notes also record William Coleman as its secretary. Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/philadelphiadire1811phil/page/n421/mode/1up Clipping: clippings/DIR_1811_p416_african-insurance-company.jpg

orgs.name: Quomony Clarkson's school, Green's Court
orgs.note: A school for children of colour in Green's Court between Spruce and Pine, established 1804. Arthur Donaldson counted about 50 scholars and a night school of about 30 in October 1811, and 31 boys and 19 girls on May 12, 1813 (The Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).

orgs.name: Solomon Clarkson's school, Lombard Street
orgs.note: A school for children of colour in Lombard Street, established by Solomon Clarkson on October 27, 1812; 19 boys and 5 girls on May 12, 1813 (The Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).

orgs.name: John Gloucester's school, Seventh below Shippen
orgs.note: John Gloucester's school for children of colour in Seventh Street below Shippen, by his Presbyterian church, established 1810; 16 boys and 11 girls on May 12, 1813 (The Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).

orgs.name: Ruth Hand's school, Race Street
orgs.note: A school in Race Street teaching reading and sewing, supported by a fund belonging to the Episcopal Church under three trustees, established about 1786; 7 boys and 29 girls on May 12, 1813 (The Juvenile Magazine, July 1813).

orgs.name: Pay schools taught by colored teachers (1838)
orgs.note: The 1838 Abolition Society report lists ten pay schools taught by colored teachers, with 288 scholars on their rolls and 260 attending. 'M. and S. Gordon' are Martha B. and Sarah Ann Gordon of 57 Pine Street. Source: https://archive.org/details/presentstatecond00penn/page/29/mode/2up
